messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
At 76, Arthur sat quietly in his modest living room, the walls adorned with faded photographs of a life once full of joy. A widower for the last five years, he found himself increasingly alone, wrestling with the shadows of memories that seemed to come alive in his mind. The most potent of those memories stemmed from his harrowing experiences as a civilian in a war zone decades ago, an event that forever altered his perception of safety and trust. The chaos of gunfire and the sight of bodies littering the streets haunted him; he could still vividly recall the day he had to flee for his life, the panic consuming him as he ran, leaving behind the familiarity of home. Each recollection was like a film reel that played in his mind, the images sharp but devoid of feeling, as if they belonged to someone else. When he thought about that day, he felt an unsettling numbness wash over him, a stark contrast to the terror he had lived.

In the years following the trauma, Arthur's interpretation of the world around him shifted dramatically. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, filled with potential threats lurking in every corner. This belief reinforced his sense of vulnerability and helplessness, leading him to distance himself from others. As he watched people in his everyday life—whether in the grocery store where he worked as a cashier or during his rare trips to the park—he scrutinized their every movement, anticipating danger in their gestures. His belief that the world was filled with threats made him hyper-aware of any potential risks, leading him to constantly assess every situation as dangerous, which kept his anxiety levels high and further entrenched his need to avoid social interactions. His hypervigilance had become a constant companion, an internal alarm system that never quieted. It was exhausting, yet he felt he had no choice; staying alert was the only way he could keep himself safe. This need for vigilance also disrupted his sleep, as he lay awake for hours, unable to relax enough to surrender to rest, constantly on guard for signs of potential harm. To combat the relentless anxiety and memories that surfaced each night, Arthur found himself staying up later, believing that exhaustion would shield him from the intrusive thoughts that haunted him.

Arthur's memories often spiraled into a cycle of negative thoughts that left him feeling defeated. He thought about why the war had happened to him, replaying the events in his mind, trying to make sense of the senselessness. This rumination deepened his negative appraisals, reinforcing the idea that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. Gone were the days when he felt vibrant and alive; now, he often felt like a shadow of his former self. This conviction that he was permanently altered fed into his memories, making them more vivid and harder to escape, as if he were stuck reliving the moments that reinforced his sense of loss. Arthur pushed away any positive feelings that dared to surface, convinced they were unsafe. He feared that allowing himself to feel joy would only lead to further pain. This avoidance strategy became a refuge, isolating him from the warmth of human connection and further entrenching his belief that he could no longer trust anyone or anything. Over time, avoiding connections with others shaped his memories, as he found himself suppressing any positive interactions, which only strengthened the vivid recollections of his traumatic past that he desperately tried to escape.

As the months stretched into years, Arthur's coping mechanisms led to an increasing withdrawal from driving. The simple act of getting behind the wheel filled him with dread, as he recalled the moments when violence erupted near his home in the war zone. The thought of being in a vehicle—a place where he felt trapped—triggered memories that made him feel as if he were reliving that terrifying day. Instead of confronting these feelings, he chose to avoid driving altogether, believing he was safeguarding himself, but in reality, it only reinforced his sense of incapacity and isolation. The perceived threat of being in a vehicle brought back overwhelming memories of panic and fear from his past, and avoiding driving seemed like the only logical way to protect himself from those feelings. This self-imposed exile from the world deepened his negative appraisals, making him feel more disconnected and vulnerable.

Now, sitting in his living room, Arthur felt a mixture of fear and hope as he finally sought help. The weight of his past was heavy, and he understood that he was caught in a cycle that seemed unbreakable. Yet, there was a flicker of desire for change, a yearning to reclaim some semblance of the life he had lost. He was terrified that the path ahead would be too painful, but the thought of continuing to live in his own prison filled him with dread. Arthur hoped that by reaching out, he might begin to unravel the threads of his memories and fears, finding a way to breathe again in a world he had come to see as perilous.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not illustrate how negative appraisals influence or lead to memory, leaving this edge missing.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: There is no indication of how perceived threat influences or leads to maladaptive strategies, making this edge absent.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The narrative does not convey how maladaptive strategies influence or lead to memory, resulting in a missing edge.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: It is not demonstrated how maladaptive strategies impact or lead to negative appraisals, leaving this edge unfulfilled.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
As he watched people in his everyday life—whether in the grocery store where he worked as a cashier or during his rare trips to the park—he scrutinized their every movement, anticipating danger in their gestures. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This hyper-vigilance had begun to warp his perception, feeding into a belief that he was weak and vulnerable, which made the memories of the trauma more accessible and vivid, as if they were always just beneath the surface waiting to resurface.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The thought of being in a vehicle—a place where he felt trapped—triggered memories that made him feel as if he were reliving that terrifying day. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When the threat of being in a car felt this close, it only made sense to avoid driving altogether, as each time he got behind the wheel, he felt the pull of those memories bearing down on him like a weight he couldn’t shake.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The perceived threat of being in a vehicle brought back overwhelming memories of panic and fear from his past, and avoiding driving seemed like the only logical way to protect himself from those feelings. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
However, this strategy of avoidance only solidified his belief that he was incapable of facing the world, reinforcing a negative self-image that he was fragile and unable to cope with ordinary situations.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This rumination deepened his negative appraisals, reinforcing the idea that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The weight of these negative thoughts kept the memories fresh and alive, as he found himself returning to the day of the trauma, convinced that he would never escape the shadows it cast on his life.
<<<END>>>
